extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal scholars, law students, and judges interested in patent infringement and the doctrine of equivalents
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for applying the doctrine of equivalents in patent infringement cases, including tests for limiting equivalents in view of prior art, the role of technological change, and comparative international approaches (notably the EPC/Article 69 Protocol).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of equivalents limited by prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations in a claim cannot be given a range of equivalents so wide as to cause the claim to encompass anything in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not enlarge claims by equivalents to encompass teachings of the prior art (cases cited: Senmed v. Richard-Allen; Tandon v. USITC). This principle constrains the permissible scope of equivalents so that patent protection does not cover what was already public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee bears burden regarding prior art and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee bears the burden of showing that the range of equivalents it seeks will not encompass the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As taught in Wilson Sporting Goods, a patentee asserting equivalents must demonstrate that the claimed range of equivalents would not read on prior art; failure to make this showing undermines an equivalents-based infringement claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical-claim (patentability) test for limits on equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A method for determining limits of claim coverage: write a hypothetical claim sufficient to literally cover the accused device and decide whether it would have been patentable over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hypothetical claim could not have been allowed by the PTO over the prior art, it is improper to permit the patentee to obtain that coverage under the doctrine of equivalents; if the hypothetical claim could have been allowed, the prior art is not a bar. This test operationalizes the prior-art constraint on equivalents (discussed in Wilson Sporting Goods and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior art under 35 U.S.C. §§102 and 103 when assessing equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Discerning the range of equivalents involves consideration of what the prior art would have anticipated (35 U.S.C. §102) and what the prior art would have made obvious (35 U.S.C. §103) at the time of the original filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of equivalents requires evaluating both anticipation and obviousness of the hypothetical coverage at the filing date; these statutory inquiries limit the permissible equivalents scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of technological advances on equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'embellishment' made possible by technological advances may not permit the accused device to escape the 'web of infringement,' but where extensive technological advances produce multiple departures from literal claim language, the totality of change may be too great to support infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize that technological progress can create unanticipated equivalents meriting protection, yet significant cumulative technical differences across claimed functions (see Texas Instruments) can defeat an equivalents finding. Evaluate both the nature and scope of departures caused by technological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the doctrine — equity and prevention of piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents was judicially devised to provide equity and to prevent 'pirating' of the patentee's invention where there is no literal infringement but liability is nevertheless appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As framed in Graver Tank and subsequent cases, the doctrine serves to protect substance over form and to prevent trivial changes from avoiding liability, while still respecting the public interest in clear claim boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine is an exception, not the default
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the doctrine of equivalents is the exception, not the rule; it should not be automatically considered in every case where literal infringement is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts warn that routine reliance on equivalents would undermine the certainty of claim language and chill competitors' ability to design around patents. Use of the doctrine must be restrained to avoid eroding public notice of claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening literal scope must be limited by public interest in certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadening the literal scope of a claim (i.e., redefining claims by equivalence) 'constitutes a deviation from the need of the public to know the precise legal limits of patent protection' and thus is admissible only to temper unsparing logic and serve justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalents can be invoked to achieve equitable outcomes, but courts must weigh this against the public's need for reliable boundaries; expansion beyond permissible interpretation is justified only to serve the doctrine's real purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific balancing by trier of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Each case in which infringement by equivalents is asserted turns on its facts and requires the trier of fact to balance competing public policies: avoiding a 'fraud on the patent' versus the public's need for reasonable certainty as to patent scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence determinations are highly fact-dependent; judges/juries must perform a balancing of policy considerations in light of the case-specific technical and legal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPC Article 69 and Protocol require an intermediate approach to claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EPC Article 69, 'the extent of the protection conferred by a European patent shall be determined by the terms of the claims,' but the description and drawings shall be used to interpret the claims; the Protocol calls for an intermediate standard combining fair protection for the patentee with reasonable certainty for third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theory Article 69 and its Protocol permit use of the doctrine of equivalents (by avoiding a strict literal-only approach), but implementation is intended to strike a middle ground between literalism and open-ended protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of international harmony in applying equivalents; national variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the doctrine of equivalents is applied in many international forums, it is not applied or interpreted harmoniously; national laws and courts often reach different results (illustrated by the Epilady litigation across UK and German courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners seeking international protection must obtain patents in each country and anticipate divergent national interpretations of equivalents; the EPC provides some harmonizing framework, but many substantive aspects remain governed by national law and adjudicated in national courts.
